author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
description:
Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas

SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon, as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket.

Starship Flight 15 is expected to orbit the Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase, in south Texas.

Continue reading...
title: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse

author: AFP
description:
Statement a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.

Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.

Continue reading...
title: Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab minority

author: Andy Bull at Stade de France
description:
• France 21-19 South Africa

  • Scrum-half key in thriller full of twists and turns

Friday night at the Stade de France may just be the best show in sport. The French had laid on a full Cecil B DeMille production: fireworks, flamethrowers, floodlights, a multicoloured drone show involving a three-storey-tall cockerel that then reassembled itself into a beating red, blue and white heart before transforming into a vast tricolore along with 150 dancers carrying LEDs who performed to an ear-splitting choral rendition of Madonna’s Like a Prayer. Astonishingly enough, what came after actually lived up to it.

It had twists and turns, a scattering of superb performances from some of the finest players in the game, a fistful of red and yellow cards, fantastic free-wheeling tries and several agonisingly intense stretches of scrummaging and defence, a clutch of hugely controversial decisions by both coaches and the referee, and one crucial missed convers
title: France cling on for furious victory against South Africa after Dupont sizzles

author: Bernie Sanders
description:
This is not a personality contest. This is a debate about the future of the Democratic party

The election for Democratic Senate leader between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen must be understood for what it is.

This is not a personality contest. This is a debate about the future of the Democratic party. It is a debate about whether the Democratic party remains a top-down party dominated by billionaire campaign contributors, inside-the-beltway consultants and 30-second TV ads, or whether we can transform it into a grassroots party of, by and for the working families of our country.

Continue reading...
title: What the choice between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen for Senate leader is all about | Bernie Sanders

author: Barney Ronay
description:
The sandpaper affair is back, and the reason it has hit Australia so hard is because it is sneaky – or basically quite English

Any plans for the weekend? Personally I’m all set. I will be watching the full Pat Cummins sandpaper denial press conference, filmed live on location in Sydney on Friday morning, and now preserved uncut and un-redacted on YouTube.

I will not speed it up, or flick through impatiently only to find myself bogged down in endless adverts for old fat guys doing military callisthenics, and pills that will dissolve the vile writhing parasites that definitely live in my guts.

Continue reading...
title: A cricketing drama to divide a nation: why the sandpaper scandal is Australia’s Bazball | Barney Ronay

author: David Hytner
description:
• England visit Madrid for first time since fan abuse in 2004

  • ‘We had the same discussion before the Serbia game’

Thomas Tuchel will remind his ­England players of the anti-racism protocols as they prepare to play Spain in Madrid for the first time since the notorious meeting between the countries in 2004. Spain won 1-0 at the Bernabéu but the occasion was ruined by racist abuse directed at England’s black players from the stands.

England have since played three games in Spain, although they refused to return to Madrid for the first of them in 2009. The match was moved to Seville. There were no ­problems in any of the three; the second was in Alicante in 2015, the third back in Seville in 2018.

Continue reading...
title: Tuchel to remind England players of anti-racism protocols before game in Spain

author: Scott Murray
description:
• Nations League updates from 7.45pm GMT kick-off

  • Live scores | Follow us on BlueSky | And email Scott

Scotland first played North Macedonia in the 2010 World Cup qualifiers. It didn’t end well. They did win the return leg at Hampden 2-1, though. The countries met again in qualification for the 2014 edition; that didn’t start well at Hampden but at least the away fix
title: Scotland v North Macedonia: Nations League – live

author: Emma Loffhagen
description:
Parents take action while independent bookshops say they had already stopped stocking his titles

In Sarah’s house, David Walliams has been a bedtime staple for years. Her children, aged eight, six and four, have dressed up as his characters for World Book Day – they love the over-the-top, unusual names and illustrations.

Now, all the books are going. “I’ll probably take them away and replace them with other authors,” says Sarah, a mother in west London. “Sooner rather than later, so they don’t realise.” If any of her children ask why, she will tell them “that his choices aren’t great and that I think we should be reading other books”.

Continue reading...
title: Families clear homes of David Walliams books after sexual offence allegations

author: Greg Wood at Cheltenham
description:
Popular chaser victorious but ground issues, horses slipping and the low sun are all negatives for Cheltenham

One of the more remarkable career records in jumping was extended again on Friday as Jonbon, one of the most popular chasers in training, won the Shloer Chase for the third time in the last four seasons and maintained his lifetime streak of never having finished outside the first two in 29 starts under National Hunt rules.

On the opening day of Cheltenham’s second-biggest meeting, though, it also felt like a somewhat flat success, out of keeping with the setting and occasion. Jonbon was left with just two rivals to beat after Gidleigh Park, the second-favourite on Friday morning, was ruled out a couple of hours before the race due to concerns about the drying ground.

Continue reading...
title: Jonbon shines on yet another trying day for troubled home of jumps racing

author: Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot
description:
No 10 sources say PM wants party to refocus on Tories as electoral threat after prioritising Reform and Greens

Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “re-arm” to fight the Conservatives at the next election amid concern inside government that they must take the prospect of a Kemi Badenoch-led recovery seriously.

Downing Street sources said the prime minister wanted Labour headquarters to refocus on the Tories as an electoral threat after more than two years of prioritising Nigel Farage’s Reform and, on their left flank, the Greens.

Continue reading...
title: Andy Burnham urges Labour to ‘re-arm’ for Kemi Badenoch comeback

author: Martin Rowson
description: Continue reading...
title: Martin Rowson on the downfall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang – cartoon

author: Boyd Tonkin
description:
Intrepid writer and journalist who reported on the Troubles and Watergate, and whose string of bestsellers began with The Surgeon of Crowthorne

The author and journalist Simon Winchester, who has died after a heart attack aged 82, thought himself lucky to have enjoyed “a pretty interesting, world-wandering life”. Those wanderings yielded a harvest of 30 books across a vast spectrum of subjects: from the land beneath to the wind above; from earthquakes to dictionaries, oceans to engines.

The globe-trotting polymath, an American citizen from 2011, loved to take an everyday “invisible thing” in culture or nature – such as the winds of his final book, The Breath of the Gods (2025) – and show how it shapes private and public histories. We first knew about the Chornobyl disaster, which hastened the end of the USSR and a new geopolitical order, because an aberrant wind allowed Swedish scientists to measure the radioactive fallout freakishly blowing from Ukraine.
title: Simon Winchester obituary

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an article by Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett in which she questions why it took so long to unmask Russell Brand and David Walliams

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is correct when she talks about the toxic 1990s in the media industry (Why did it take so long to unmask Brand and Walliams? Because noughties culture told girls like me abuse was normal, 11 November). This abhorrent sexualised behaviour from celebrities and channel executives has been going on for much longer.

When I worked in the media as a makeup artist in the 1980s we were warned never to be alone if working with a certain Mr Savile or Mr Harris. Men like those two were the majority, not a minority. They were directly enabled by those managers and directors who sanctioned their behaviour through inaction. If you complained, you were seen as trouble and hounded out.
title: Toxic media industry must face a reckoning | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
An investigator writes that a human-written grievance at least gets to the heart of the issue immediately. Plus letters from Dexter Jandoo and Pete Bibby

Re your article (‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints, 8 November), I’m a complaint investigator for a housing association. I’ve worked here for nine years, and the scope of my job has completely changed within a few months. I am well-versed in policy and legislation, and I love my job, but it can be unbearable sifting through hundreds of pages of extremely wordy complaints.

You only need to look at the awful case of Awaab Ishak to know how important it is that a housing provider’s complai
title: How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Saul Abbott says his pace of presenting matched the pace of the world surrounding him, Jane Bates values Gardeners’ World immeasurably, while Joe Mackenzie shares a poignant memory

I started my professional gardening career in 2004, a year after Monty started presenting Gardeners’ World (‘It’s the final goodbye’: Monty Don bows out with a blissful last Gardeners’ World, 6 November).

To say this great man taught me much of what I have learned since is a gross understatement. Not just about the principles and practices of gardening itself, but the understanding in a greater sense of what a garden is, what it gives to us both in bounty, tangibly, and nourishment of something far greater, internally.
title: Monty Don was the best teacher and presenter imaginable | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose

The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence (The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November).

The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences.
title: The folly of just-in-time supply chains | Letters

author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
description:
Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to entice shoppers

The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?

Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.

Continue reading...
title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank

author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer in Fayetteville, Georgia
description:
• Coach was ‘transparent’ in dealings with club, federation

  • Pochettino had signed deal to stay with US through 2030

There were always going to be tears at Mauricio Pochettino’s news conference at US Soccer’s national training center on Friday. It was only a matter of when. Pochettino is famously emotional, and nobody in attendance had to wait long for the waterworks – they came during his introductory remarks, as he thanked the US Soccer executives flanking him for the opportunity to guide the US men. He grew emotional again as he addressed his impending departure for Manchester United, one announced just hours earlier.

“I think [the decision was],” Pochettino said, pausing to compose himself, “one of the most difficult decisions of our careers. Thank you guys. Thank you so much.”

Continue reading...
title: Tearful Pochettino says United job was ‘difficult to turn down’ in USMNT farewell

author: Alan Martin
description:
We put 32 electric toothbrushes to the test, from oscillating Oral-B models to sustainable brands like Suri, to find the best for cleaning power and value for money

• How to make your toothbrush last longer

If you grew up using a conventional toothbrush – essentially a stick with bristles on the end – you may be surprised to learn just how long the electric toothbrush has been around. The first was designed in the late 1930s, but that model was a long way from the sleek, feature-packed and Bluetooth-enabled beasts you can buy today.

There are now dozens of ultra-advanced versions on the market, but which ones are worth your cash? To help answer that question, my teeth have become figurative guinea pigs. Over the past two years, I’ve put 32 electric toothbrushes from the likes of Dyson, Oral-B, Philips, Suri, Ordo, Silk’n and For
title: The best electric toothbrushes in the UK for every budget

author: Alex Bellos
description:
Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems

The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.

After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

author: Ugo Monye
description:
Steve Borthwick has picked a team to excite fans – let’s see them beat the Brave Blossoms at their own game on Saturday

Based on England’s performance last week, there was part of me that thought about writing a piece that would light another fire under the squad. As predicted a week ago, England were galvanised by events leading up to the game against Australia and I cannot remember the last time when I came away from Twickenham so impressed by both the result and the performance.

Pretty much every box was ticked. It was a complete showing. Discipline was on point, the set piece went well and England scored all manner of tries. The question is, how does a much-changed team take a step up, continue to b
title: England have licence to thrill against Japan after acing audition against Australia | Ugo Monye

author: Jasper Jolly
description:
JLR chief executive calls for EU and Britain to join forces amid competition from Chinese electric carmakers

Jaguar Land Rover has reported a £451m quarterly loss as it counts the cost of cutting 4,000 jobs, while its chief executive has called for the EU and Britain to work together in the face of competition from China.

Britain’s largest automotive employer reported revenues rising to £5.9bn between July and September, but it recorded £530m in costs from the job cuts announced near the end of that period amid tough trading conditions.

Continue reading...
title: Jaguar Land Rover reports £451m quarterly loss after cutting 4,000 jobs

author: John Crace
description:
Saintly heir to the throne breaks his hectic schedule for a magazine lowdown on life in the country

Country Life: Guest Edited by HRH the Prince of Wales

Front Cover: Photo of me outdoors. I love the country, me.

Continue reading...
title: Sheds, cakes and photos of me – Prince William’s Country Life, digested by John Crace

author: Lauren Cochrane
description:
From Calvin Klein to British Vogue, the Real Madrid man is leading the way when it comes to football’s foray into fashion. But is he playing it safe?

This Sunday, Jude Bellingham will line up with his England teammates for a match against Spain. But the footballer has been hitting the headlines way beyond the pitch recently – thanks to fronting a Calvin Klein underwear ad released this month, and becoming the first footballer to appear solo on the cover of British Vogue.

It’s a savvy move for the 23-year-old, future-proofing himself as a power player both on and off the pitch. This is a roadmap carved out by David Beckham, who since retiring in 2013 has become a brand and personality that transcends sport. Beckham – together with his wife, Victoria – became a billionaire this year.
title: Branding it like Beckham: how Jude Bellingham is future-proofing his fame

author: Robert Kitson
description:
Steve Borthwick is ringing the changes and George Ford, despite his 108 caps, also knows he needs to perform

In Tokyo this week the police have been seeking to help newly arrived visitors from overseas. Several local bar and restaurant managers have been arrested for targeting and ripping off unwary tourists who had walked into their establishments in good faith. Unfortunately for Japan’s rugby players, as they prepare to enter England’s chilly lair, there is no such reciprocal deal to protect them from a collective south-west London mugging on Saturday afternoon.

Instead they will be required to fend for themselves, with the odds heavily stacked in the home team’s favour. England have racked up a half-century of points against the Brave Blossoms in both their two most recent meetings – and that was before rugby’s try-scoring rates began ratcheting upwards. Japan’s arrival also neatly intersects with their hosts’ desire to build on the momentum of
title: Ojomoh and Pollock get their shot as England’s World Cup hopefuls aim to crush Japan

author: Matthew Pearce and Pippa Neill
description:
Exclusive: Government in ‘private meetings’ about removing cost cap protections under Aarhus convention

  • UK politics live – latest updates

The government is considering stripping back legal protections that limit the costs community groups face when challenging planning decisions that threaten nature.

The Aarhus convention, an environmental treaty that was signed into law by the UK in 2005, guarantees the legal right to participate in democratic processes on environmental matters – such as sewage pollution, new roads or datacentre developments.

Continue reading...
title: Right to make green challenges to planning decisions under threat, say UK lawyers

author: Anna Betts
description:
Gunman killed one person and injured at least four others in and around condo building not far from the White House

More details were emerging on Friday about the previous morning’s shooting in north-west Washington DC, as a manager in the shooter’s residential building told how he was angry over living conditions there and confessed to the killings.

The gunman killed one person and injured at least four others on Thursday in and around the condominium building in the Logan Circle neighborhood of the capital, not far from the White House, where he lived.

Continue reading...
title: Doctor named as DC gym shooting suspect confessed, detailing dispute over living conditions, police say

author: Brigid Schulte and Haley Swenson
description:
Amid concerns over the influence of the manosphere, our findings show that young men are concerned about caregiving

When young men helped propel Donald Trump into the White House in 2024, the administration doubled down on a brand of toxic masculinity popular in the so-called manosphere.

They touted high testosterone, male supremacy, and a “biblically-based family” where men work and provide, and deferential women stay home to bear children and care for others.

Continue reading...
title: Young men were key to the blue wave. Our research offers a reason why | Brigid Schulte and Haley Swenson

author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
description:
Judge imposes three-year treatment order on Donaldson for aiding and abetting sexual offences by her husband, Jeffrey

Jeffrey Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, has been placed on the sex offender register for five years for aiding and abetting sexual offences by her disgraced husband.

Eleanor Donaldson appeared via remote link at Newry crown court to hear the order on Friday one month after her husband, the former Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, was convicted of abusing two women when they were children.

Continue reading...
title: Eleanor Donaldson, wife of former DUP leader, placed on sex offender register

author: Jonathan Jones
description:
Nicole Eisenman hits the coast, Scotland remembers its Roman days, while Wolfgang Tillmans and Tracey Emin get romantic – all in your weekly dispatch

Nicole Eisenman
A free display beside the seaside from the witty and imaginative sort-of-figurative artist.
• Turner Contemporary, Margate, from 14 November to 11 April

Continue reading...
title: Kisses galore, seaside shenigans, McRoman adventures and street feats – the week in art

author: Suzanne Wrack
description:
Neither side have lost in the league yet but a more competitive division should take title race to the wire

There was a time when the games between the top three – traditionally Chelsea, Manchester City and Arsenal – were title-deciding games. Where every point taken off a title rival was key. Such was the gap in investment and quality between those teams and the rest of the Women’s Super League that it was extremely rare that points would be dropped to teams outside that elite clique.

As the WSL has grown in investment, profile and size, that narrative has started to shift a little. The investment gap is still large from the top to the bottom of the league, but increased investment among the “best of the rest” and even among those teams further down the table, as well as an increase in high-quality coaches with the tactical and technical vision to get more from players, is having an impact.
title: Why Chelsea and Manchester City’s WSL clash is not as season-defining as you think

author: Geoff Lemon
description:
The Test captain kept his promise to answer all questions at a press conference that made his position clear and filled some but not all gaps

Our coverage on Thursday said that Pat Cummins needed to front up, and nobody can fairly say that he didn’t. It was a proper ’til-they-drop affair from Australia’s cricket captain, an hour and 10 minutes at a press conference podium taking questions about the 2018 ball-tampering episode until every journalist present ran out of steam. You might have expected some partial concession to teammate Usman Khawaja’s depiction of endemic cheating, but Cummins was firm that this did not reflect the life he’d known. Once more with feeling, but more importantly with
title: Cummins stands firm on ball tampering to leave Australian cricket back where it started | Geoff Lemon

author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
description:
Siberian rubythroat was thousands of miles off course from its route to winter in south or south-east Asia

A bird that flies south from its breeding grounds in Siberia to winter in south and south-east Asia has been found thousands of miles off course in Cumbria. Regrettably, it was found by a cat.

Chris Hind, Cumbria’s county recorder for birds, said it was “extraordinary” that a Siberian rubythroat was found on his patch, albeit dead. There have been only 17 recorded instances of the bird in the UK, 15 of those in the northern Scottish isles.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Incredibly unusual’ bird migrating from Siberia found in Cumbria – killed by cat

author: Tim Byrne
description:
When founder Shay Leighton put fliers in tattoo parlours, barbers and boxing gyms in Australia, men quickly responded – then it went global. But why do some feel such baggage about books?

“When did we decide that men and reading and toughness all had to be separate things?” Shay Leighton asks over a pint of Melbourne Black in his local Brunswick pub. “I don’t know about you, but I didn’t get a vote.”

For 14 years, Leighton has run the Tough Guy Book Club, a not-for-profit charity dedicated to encouraging men to read – although he’s quick to stress that they do more than just that. “We’re not a reading club, we’re a talking club,” he says. “The three goals of book club are: read more, talk more, have more friends.”

Continue reading...
title: Pride and no prejudice: how Tough Guy Book Club taught 10,000 men to be unashamed of reading

author: Rachael Sigee
description:
This coming-of-age tale of Catholic school girls is gleefully camp from the off – and full of fun references to its 2004 setting. And then a Halloween party goes wrong…

What’s more judgmental than a teenage girl? Easy: the Catholic church. Deliciously, Netflix’s new YA drama The Body has both in equal measure. It’s Halloween 2004 at St Mark’s Catholic school and the social hierarchy is exactly as you would expect. Perched at the top is the dance troupe, the Lions, presided over by Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany), two best friends skirting around their sexual chemistry. The show’s resident outcasts are Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) and Leo (Jackson Kelly), previously homeschooled siblings who live a limited existence with their unwell mother. Leo seems like a harmless weirdo (or do his disturbing drawings suggest otherwise?) while Lisbeth is a classic loser desperate to ingratiate herself with the cool crowd.

Her opportunity arises when she’s invited to a Hall
title: The Body review – this sexy retro high school drama is like Cruel Intentions … with added Satanic rituals

author: Eddy Frankel
description:
Sainsbury Museum and Art Centre, Norwich
With some uplifting works despite a certain obviousness, this broad double-hander tackles the vast topics of love, smooching and the aftermath

To quote 1980s soft rockers Foreigner, I want to know what love is. And I want the Sainsbury Centre to show me. This big winter series tackles love in all its guises – and for now comprises two shows, one about smooching called The Last Human Kiss, another about desire and heartbreak called Ecstasy and the Aftermath.

The problem is, love is probably the biggest topic in human history, let alone art history. Think of the endless novels and poems and films; think of how many songs have been written, how many paintings painted. Love is an endlessly vast topic and this show barely scratches its surface.

C
title: A lipsmacking journey from kisses galore to tears of despair – How Do We Find Love? review

author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
description:
Singer, 76, was in Manchester with his band for penultimate UK show of his Songs in the Key of Life anniversary tour

When Stevie Wonder’s team just called to say: “Can we all come to your restaurant in Stalybridge at 11pm on a Sunday?” Ryan Robinson, of course, said yes.

First the band turned up, and then – at 12.30am – the man himself arrived. Hours later, staff at the Cafe Continental were sharing a £1,000 tip.

Continue reading...
title: ‘So lovely’: Stevie Wonder surprises Stalybridge restaurant with late-night visit and £1,000 tip

author: Alexandra Coghlan
description:
Royal Festival Hall, London
With this programme of Strauss (Johann II and Richard) and Mozart – and Emanuel Ax the deft and lucid soloist – Manfred Honeck, who joins as principal conductor in 2028, gave an exciting statement of intent

‘I am a man of tradition,” Manfred Honeck, the Philharmonia’s new principal conductor designate, declared earlier this week in rehearsals. But for the 68-year-old Austrian, who in 2028 becomes only the seventh principal conductor in the ensemble’s 81-year history, it’s tradition as defined by Mahler: “Not the worship of the ashes but the preservation of fire.” It was a fire in full blaze by the end of last night’s concert – a scorching taste of things to come.

Even if you couldn’t see Honeck smiling at his musicians, or them smiling back, you could hear it in a Fledermaus Overture that could barely keep t
title: Philharmonia/Honeck/Ax review – principal conductor designate gives a scorching taste of things to come

author: Andrew Pulver
description:
Reports that the star – the most high-profile of the final five contenders – has been offered favourable contract terms hint that Amazon MGM may want him as its first 007

Robert Pattinson has emerged as the favourite in the race to succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond, according to a credible film-industry source.

Writing in Puck, Matthew Belloni suggests that the favourable contract terms he says have been offered to Pattinson suggest that the actor, currently in cinemas with reality-crime thriller Primetime, is studio Amazon MGM’s preferred choice for the role.

Continue reading...
title: Robert Pattinson reportedly leads James Bond contenders

author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
description:
Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’

The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis.

Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows.

Continue reading...
title: UK’s biggest insurer hit by rise in subsidence claims after record hot summer

author: Will Hayward
description:
As the main opposition in the Senedd, the party should be taking politics seriously. Spoiler alert: it’s not

In May 2026, Reform UK became the official opposition inside the Welsh Senedd. It was the best result the party had ever received in a national parliament – and since that time it has been a wild ride. Given that its leader, Nigel Farage, claims he expects to one day lead the UK government, how it performs in Wales matters more than just for the people of Cymru; it gives the rest of the UK a sense of what it could expect if Reform does well in the next general election.

Just to give you a taste, here are two developments. In September, Reform’s leader in Wales, Dan Thomas, resigned after he was arrested and r
title: If you’re wondering what a Reform government might look like, just look at its chaotic record in Wales | Will Hayward

author: Ali Martin at the Optus Stadium, Perth
description:
• England dismissed for just 131 in opening ODI in Perth

  • McCullum: ‘KP’s message will be measured but firm’


Brendon McCullum has backed Kevin Pietersen to help educate England’s batting lineup before the “­specialist mentor” he hired in the summer leaves the tour of Australia after Sunday’s second one-day ­international in Adelaide.

The collapse to 131 all out for a seven-wicket defeat in Perth on Friday naturally brought back memories of the first Ashes Test 12 months ago. But more relevant is what it means should a similarly fast, bouncy surface – such as at the Wanderers in Johannesburg – be encountered during next year’s 50-over World Cup in southern Africa.

Continue r
title: McCullum backs Pietersen to help England after collapse on ‘trampoline’ pitch

author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer and Will Unwin
description:
• Pochettino to take charge of two final USMNT matches

  • He has signed two-and-a-half-year United contract

Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from the US men’s national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday.

The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades. United have won one of their past 11 games and are in the Premier League’s relegation zone.

Continue re
title: Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from USA to Manchester United confirmed

author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
description:
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months.

“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”

Continue reading...

description:
An innovator in mara, the fast, sample-heavy dance music of neighbourhood parties, the Nigerian has made a debut album that will be relentlessly energising

From Lagos, Nigeria
Recommended if you like Rema, Blnde, Zinoleesky
Up next Debut album Mara Gram, released 12 November; plays Nyege Nyege festival, Uganda, 19–22 November

Azzi on the Beat doesn’t exactly ease listeners into Mara Gram. On its opening track Police Way, sirens blare, drums clatter and another rhythm seems to barge in before the first has finished. This is mara, the fast, sample-heavy dance music that grew out of carnivals and neighbourhood parties in working-class Lagos, with tempos reaching 160 beats per minute.

author: Andrew Pulver
description:
As Amazon MGM Studios prepares to announce the next 007, much rides on how the news is broken. From double bookings to health and safety embarrassments, we look back at how not to do it

And then there were five. While nothing has been officially announced, it is widely understood that the shortlist to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond is now down to a handful of actors: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult.

The hunt for a new Bond comes at a propitious moment for the franchise as a whole, 25 films in (not counting the two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983). After Daniel Craig stood down from the role after completing No Time to Die (in which Bond appeared to be killed in a missile strike),
title: ‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong

author: John Crace
description:
At some point even Liz won’t remember why she’s there. Meanwhile, Nige wants more air time, and Boris Johnson couldn’t have made less effort

Like most people, I assume, I had always thought the Remembrance Sunday service at the Cenotaph was a time to think of those who died in the two world wars and later armed conflicts. It turns out that Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform, sees it differently. I was listening to Dicky being interviewed on the Jeremy Kyle show on TalkTV – Yes, I know, I’ve only myself to blame – when suddenly he went into a tirade on the BBC’s coverage of the service. His principal complaint was that Nigel Farage had not been given enough air time, though he later morphed into a rant about antisemitism. I never did quite work out how the two were meant to be linked. I’m sure the BBC will reflect seriously on this lapse of judgment in its debrief of the programme and will next year have several cameras trained on Nige throughout the service. It should
title: Digested week: do we really have to see Liz Truss at the Cenotaph for the next 30 years?

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says speed restrictions on Starshield system made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down drones

Russia has attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said speed restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield system had made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down enemy drones.

Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building.

It has been suggested that women with stories to tell felt silenced after signing non-disclosure agreements

The UK’s minister for women has suggested that the government has not gone far enough in tackling the abusive use of non-disclosure agreements.

Bridget Phillipson was commenting in the context of the allegations of improper behaviour by David Walliams – which he denies – and the conviction of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault. In both cases, it has been suggested that women with stories to tell felt silenced after signing an NDA.

Police called to Huddersfield University on Tuesday after women reported being ‘approached and grabbed’

A 29-year-old man has been charged after seven women reported being sexually assaulted on the Huddersfield University campus over a 30 minute period.

West Yorkshire police said Sophan Akbash had been charged with nine counts of sexual assault and would appear at Leeds magistrates court on Friday. Security staff called officers to Huddersfield University on Tuesday evening after reports of a man approaching and sexually touching women on and near the campus, police said.

title: Man charged after seven women sexually assaulted in 30 minutes on UK campus

author: Taz Ali
description:
Senator Van Hollen says midterm results show Americans want change in Washington, and Democrats need new leadership to deliver that

Good morning, and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Barely a week after sweeping to a stunning midterm victory, Democrats have found themselves facing an altogether different battle, one within their own ranks.

We saw a huge outburst of democracy on election day – red states, blue states, purple states – and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption, his wars and his cruelty, it was also about a call for a larger change, to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favour of the very wealthy against working people, and it’s fuelled by a corrupt political system.

The call was to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual, and to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That wi
title: Van Hollen takes aim at Schumer as Democrats face first big test after midterms – US politics live

description:
• England prevail 50-38 over France in Wollongong final

  • Joe Coyd scores four tries to set England up for glory

England successfully completed their defence of the wheelchair Rugby League World Cup after edging old foes France in a thrilling final in Wollongong.

The two best sides in the wheelchair discipline were perhaps always destined to meet in the final given the superiority they possess over the other nations. England defeated the French by only four points in Manchester four years ago in front of 5,000 fans and Tom Coyd’s side were victorious once again, this time on Australian soil.

Aaron Bower’s full report to follow

title: Rugby League World Cup glory again for England’s wheelchair champions

author: Tom Ambrose
description:
The report on food and emissions comes ahead of a joint UK-EU summit next week

Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.

There will be a “growing pressure” for parliament to scrutinise EU legislation under new deals on food and emissions to be sealed ahead of the UK’s summit with the bloc next week, a Lords’ committee has warned.

Although important details remain to be determined of the legal and institutional form that dynamic alignment will take, its introduction will mark a major change to the nature of the UK-EU relationship as it exists under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement.

As the UK aligns with more EU law, parliament will face growing pressure to scrutinise significant volumes of EU legislation.

I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe.

The deal is not done, and there’ll be some long nights ahead in the next seven days.
title: UK-EU deal will lead to ‘growing pressure’ for parliament to scrutinise legislation, warns committee – UK politics live

author: Steven Morris
description:
WellFed participants in Cornwall are reporting better blood sugar levels with help of free veg, cooking and gardening

The participants admitted that throughout their life, their food choices had been far from ideal: egg and chips, hearty roasts, raw fry – a Cornish one-pan dish of bacon, potatoes and onions, often fried in lard and once beloved of miners and fishers.

But here they were, at a community orchard in the harbourside town of St Ives in south-west Cornwall, massaging Swiss chard (to soften the leaves), dicing carrots, adding lentils into a pot to create a low-GI, high-fibre – and tasty – shepherd’s bake.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Never thought I’d eat that’: how vegetable prescriptions are helping Britons with diabetes

author: Arif Hasan
description:
Despite all the advantages offenses have secured over the years, defenses are better at pressuring the QB than any other time in recent history

The Baltimore Ravens are preparing to start their fourth quarterback this year, Jacoby Brissett, against the beleaguered Los Angeles Chargers on Monday, because of injuries to Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley and Joe Fagnano. That puts them dangerously close to the NFL record of five within a single season (a record shared by the 1984 Bears and 2023 Browns when excluding the 1987 strike season).

Jackson, Huntley and Fagnano were all injured after taking hits in games. And if it seems like quarterbacks are taking punishment more often this year, your eyes aren’t deceiving you. Through nine weeks, quarterbacks have been hit on 15.1% of their dropbacks, the most we’ve seen since 2006, when hits were first logged in official box scores.
title: NFL quarterbacks are under more pressure than ever from rushers. Why?

Léa Seydoux – who never seems to make a bad film – stars as musician Lucy, based in the countryside outside Munich with her film-maker spouse Philip (Laurence Rupp) and their young son Johnny (Malo Blanchet). description:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand next round of negotiations to include European countries

in Dublin

EU leaders will continue talks on their diplomatic and financial support for Ukraine today, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged them to “pay attention” to Vladimir Putin’s demands on security.

“There is no need to reinvent the wheel. Europe had a functioning European security architecture until it was first, gradually undermined, and ultimately destroyed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”

“In terms of the wider point, there was a very strong feeling that you know, Russian demands to put the question of European security architecture or European security arrangements into this negotiation – that is not up for negotiation... It is for Europe to decide its own arrangements. Europe and Europe alone. And again, I am talking in the wider sense when I say that.”
title: Leaders meet in Dublin amid search for lead EU negotiator for peace talks with Russia - Europe live

description:
(Erased Tapes)
Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation

Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr, in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir.

On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mour
title: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month

author: Adrian Horton
description:
The Oscar winner plays a singer turned detective searching for her niece in an overly generic Nashville-based mystery that fails to find its footing

Given the popularity of its music and the streaming services’ interest in faith-based programming, I’m always a little surprised that there aren’t more movies and TV shows about Nashville. Well, at least the idea of Nashville, the country music mecca that is perpetually struggling to define itself within and against the country at large, a place that has always been more diverse than its reputation yet still stands for a certain image of white, Christian Americana. There are plenty of enduring contradictions to mine there – the hyper-masculine men singing with their hearts on their sleeve, the Madonna-badass complex among its relatively few female stars, the suburban money in a genre ostensibly speaking to the rural common man.

Netflix seems to be aiming for some of those complexities with Heartland, a patchy neo-noir thril
title: Heartland review – Jessica Chastain’s Netflix country music thriller is more miss than hit

author: Leonard Barden
description:
The Norwegian world No 1 will be among 500 competitors in the 10-round contest of 15-minute games

Magnus Carlsen makes a very rare appearance in an open tournament on 5-6 December when the Norwegian, who has topped the world rankings for 15 successive years, competes in the 10-round Super Rapid at the XTX Markets London Classic. The venue is the Novotel West at Hammersmith and the time limit is 15 minutes per player for the entire game, plus a 10 seconds increment for each move.

In 2025, 267 players entered the Super Rapid. On Monday, when Carlsen’s participation was announced, the entry doubled in just 12 hours and is now close to 400. The capacity is 500 and Alex Holowczak, the Chief Arbiter, expects that figure to be reached this weekend or early next week. His advice to anyone contemplating entry is to do so as soon as possible to avoid disappointment. The link to the entry form is here.
title: Chess: Carlsen comes to town with tantalising tests for London Classic Super Rapid

author: Simon Jenkins
description:
For all the supposed improvements, inspectors still obsess over statistics and adjectives, but surely school success depends on teachers and parents

The government regulation of state schools by Ofsted in England is a fiasco. Following the 2023 suicide of the Reading headteacher Ruth Perry, after her school was downgraded from outstanding to inadequate, Ofsted appears to have referred to a dictionary. Single words were replaced by colour-coded report cards, which use a wider range of different adjectives to grade abstractions such as personal development and wellbeing, achievement and leadership. Never has the concept of “education” seemed so empty.

The reaction of the teaching profession to the new code has itself been devastating, as highlighted in a recent survey
title: Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve | Simon Jenkins

Her truly remarkable, Sade-ish voice is hypnotic against some dizzyingly plush production, but a modern spin on 80s pastiche sometimes veers too close to tribute

Swedish-Iranian singer Snoh Aalegra has previously described her music – a lush, pastiche-y mix of R&B, hip-hop, soul and pop – as “cinematic soul”. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies, made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like th

author: Emma John
description:
Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award revivals a healthy revival

It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player. You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball.

These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Association launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, wit
title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John

author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
description:
Suspect held in New York jail has been linked to handler behind Iran-linked operations in Britain

When the US took custody of Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi in May, investigators hoped the string of terror and arson attacks he was accused of promoting and directing against American and Jewish targets in the UK and Europe on behalf of Iran would stop. They were wrong.

An updated indictment, released on Tuesday by the US Department of Justice, describes some of what happened next. It reveals that al-Saadi has two allies, believed to be in Iran, also trying to provoke fear and chaos in the UK – one of whom is accused of orchestrating the September incident at RAF Fairford.

Continue reading...
title: US terror case sheds light on RAF Fairford arrests mystery

description:
A timely tech-bro takedown based on Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison’s real-life love affair and scandalous cryptocurrency, and the teen cannibal saga concludes. Plus: an entirely baffling Melania documentary

For this ripped-from-the-headlines tech bro drama, Netflix have coaxed their go-to chameleon Julia Garner (Inventing Anna, Ozark) into mastering another accent and rifling through the wig cupboard. Anthony Boyle (House of Guinness, Say Nothing) is Sam Bankman-Fried while Garner plays Caroline Ellison in a retelling of the pair’s real-life love affair and the rise and fall of their scandal-hit cryptocurrency, FTX. Next to the likes of HBO Max’s The Audacity, The Altruists can feel a little staid and even dated (nods to Tony Blair and Harry Potter don’t help). But all the same, its cautionary tale of myopic tech idealists fuelled by a love of extreme risk-taking feel

author: Miranda Bryant, Ignatius Ssuuna and Xiaoying You
description:
Owning an electric car, driving an electric motorbike taxi, riding scooters – we speak to people in Oslo, Kigali and Shanghai about their everyday routines

The race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world.

The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey, the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries.
title: ‘I spend less, that’s all that matters’: life in the world’s most electrified countries

Jared Kushner says move will allow talks to address ‘broader postwar European security arrangements’; Putin refuses to soften territorial demands. What we know on day 1,724

Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include European countries, Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said late on Thursday, after meeting Russian president Vladimir Putin. “This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner ​said ​later on X. “We are also working toward ‌what would be the largest prisoner ​exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people ⁠with their families.”

author: Barney Ronay at Wembley
description:
The Ballon d’Or validated the forward’s career and he extended his incredible record for England with yet another goal on his 126th appearance

Happy Harry Kane day! And many happy Harry returns. There is a process in clinical psychology known as semantic satiation. Subjects are asked to repeat a word or phrase so many times that it loses any kind of meaning. Suddenly “daffodils” is just an absurd, empty set of sounds. So it was in the buildup to Harry Kane’s record-breaking 126th cap, at the end of Harry Kane Ballon d’Or fortnight, as Harry Kane’s England were led out by top scorer Harry Kane, climax to a week of Harry Kane tributes, Harry Kane montages, 26-page Harry Kane … wait. Where were we?

This was that kind of occasion from start to finish, a night where you expected to look up from your desk mid-match to see Kane’s head looming helpfully over your shoulder, to enter the Wembley toilets at half-time and find him silently offering you a breath mint and a scented t
